title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to test whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. Execution used a hosted adapter with declared model gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 under shared_initial_candidate semantics (exactly one initial LLM generation per task, reused across arms); the guarded pipeline could request up to one validator‑triggered repair. We ran N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial). Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms (baseline = 240/240 safe; guarded = 240/240 safe). The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Under the registered shared_initial_candidate contract the single shared initial candidate must fail deterministic validation or trigger a repair for the guarded arm to create discordant pairs; in this run every shared candidate passed validation and no repairs were invoked, producing a degenerate paired contrast. We report the preregistered design, mapping from estimand to archived analysis outputs, execution accounting, an artifact‑grounded failure analysis of the null paired outcome, and concrete recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction:
Translating high‑level operator intent into device configurations that can be safely applied is a core NetOps objective. Recent work has shown that large language models (LLMs) can produce plausible configuration text, but text‑level correctness does not guarantee semantics needed in production networks: ordering, dependency constraints, resource protection, and transient state violations matter for safe application. Closed‑loop emulation (apply→simulate→score) can reveal these semantic failures and thus better approximate operational risk than text‑only tests [1].

Generate–validate–repair (GVR) architectures—where an LLM proposes a candidate, a deterministic verifier checks semantic invariants, and an automated repair rewrites the candidate when violations are found—are a widely proposed mitigation [2,3]. Prior empirical and systems work documents cases where validators plus repair achieve high repair coverage for syntactic and many semantic faults, but important questions remain about when a verifier causally reduces unsafe applies under distribution shift and adversarial prompts and about experimental designs that can reveal such causal effects [2,4,6].

We report a fully preregistered paired experiment that measured the preregistered estimand (absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate: guarded minus baseline) under shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial generation per task reused across arms). Because the execution archive and analysis artifacts are complete and deterministic, the numerical results reported here are traceable to the archived condition summaries, paired contingency table, and analysis logs. Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered, emulation‑grounded paired evaluation of a GVR pipeline; (2) an explicit artifact‑grounded mapping from estimand to archival analysis artifacts and parameters; and (3) a focused failure analysis explaining the degenerate paired outcome and concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations for future GVR evaluations.
sections.related_work:
Executable, emulation‑grounded NetOps benchmarks have been proposed to surface planning and workflow faults for LLM agents rather than only assessing textual fidelity; NetConfArena exemplifies this closed‑loop approach and motivates emulator‑level scoring [1]. Work on automatic configuration repair and program repair documents generate–validate patterns and shows that validators often enable effective repair coverage for many fault classes, while noting semantic coverage depends on verifier design and repair strategy [2,4]. Surveys of agentic architectures and tool augmentation synthesize verifier integration and uncertainty calibration as promising operational patterns, but emphasize that verifier coverage, adversary models, and evaluation protocols must be carefully matched to deployment risk [3,5].

Our study differs from prior evaluations in combining: (a) a predeclared paired estimand framing verifier effect as a paired difference; (b) preregistered shared_initial_candidate execution semantics; (c) emulation‑grounded deterministic scoring of final, appliable configurations; and (d) full archival of per‑call traces, validator traces, and analysis artifacts so that the exact measured estimand can be reconciled to archived outputs. These design choices trade off budgeted model calls and pairing precision against the need to exercise verifier‑triggered behavior, an empirical tradeoff we diagnose in the Results and Discussion.
sections.methodology:
Estimand and preregistration: The preregistered primary estimand is paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, defined as the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline) where unsafe_apply = 1 indicates a final configuration that would cause a semantic safety violation when applied in the emulator. The study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) and executed under the registered adapter contract described below.

Design and sampling: The experiment used a paired design with shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each of N = 240 distinct intent→configuration tasks the adapter produced exactly one initial LLM generation that was reused for both the baseline (LLM‑only) and guarded (GVR) episodes. Tasks were blocked into topology/vendor clusters and sampled deterministically by the registered generator: 144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial. The guarded pipeline could request up to one validator‑triggered repair per task per the preregistered contract.

Model, validator, and adapter contract: Execution used the declared hosted model gpt-5-mini and the deterministic verifier deterministic_netops_validator_v5; the adapter family was hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the only mechanism by which the guarded arm can change the paired outcome is (A) the shared initial candidate fails deterministic validation, prompting a repair, and the repair produces a different final configuration; or (B) the verifier flags the candidate in a way that changes final scoring. The adapter enforced at most one repair call per task.

Scoring and analysis mapping: Final outcomes were assigned by deterministic emulation and the validator trace: safe (0) or unsafe (1). The archived analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1) produced the paired contingency table, the bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729), and an exact two‑sided McNemar test on discordant pairs. The mapping between the preregistered estimand and archived fields is direct: the archived paired contingency (n11,n10,n01,n00) and the archived condition summary (baseline_success_count, guarded_success_count) are the inputs to the paired estimator and the bootstrap. Per the preregistered plan, items flagged as 'possible false‑safe' (validator PASS but emulator unsafe outcome) would be excluded from the primary analysis and analyzed in sensitivity channels; no such flags occurred in this execution.

Operational controls: The execution adhered to the preregistered retry policy for infra failures (up to two retries); no infra failures or unscorable episodes occurred. Provider‑call accounting was recorded for every model call and reconciled in the deterministic reconciliation artifact.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: The run completed as planned. Planned_episode_count = 480; completed_episode_count = 480; complete_pair_count = 240. Provider call audit recorded hosted_model_call_event_count = 240 and cache_miss_count = 240, consistent with exactly one shared initial generation per task and no additional generation calls. Model_calls_used = 240. No infra failures, no missingness, and no preregistered exclusions occurred.

Primary outcomes and contingency: Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms. The archived condition summary reports baseline_successes = 240, guarded_successes = 240 (baseline and guarded success rates = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n11 = 240, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The paired estimator (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) = 0.00. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. These numeric outputs are produced by the archived analysis executor and its outputs are available in the archived analysis artifacts.

Validator and repair activity: Validator traces show that deterministic_netops_validator_v5 validated the shared initial candidate for every task (validation_after.valid = true, violation_count = 0 in validator traces), and repair_attempts = 0 across the repair log. The reconciliation artifact records provider_call_audit.stage_counts.shared_initial_generation = 240 and all_deterministic_consistency_checks_passed = true, confirming that (a) a single shared initial generation was produced for each pair and (b) that initial candidate passed deterministic validation in every case. Because no shared initial candidate failed validation and no repairs were invoked, the guarded final configuration matched the shared candidate for all episodes and baseline and guarded outcomes are identical across all subgroups (in‑distribution, shift, adversarial). Planned sensitivity channels (possible false‑safe flags, infra‑failures treated as unsafe) were unused because no items were flagged or failed.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded explanation of the null paired contrast: Under the registered shared_initial_candidate semantics the paired contrast can only differ when the single shared initial candidate is invalidated by the verifier and a repair is applied (or when verification semantics alter final scoring). The execution artifacts show exactly one shared initial generation per task (hosted_model_call_event_count = 240; stage_counts.shared_initial_generation = 240) and a deterministic verifier PASS for every shared candidate (validator traces: valid = true, violation_count = 0). Consequently, the guarded arm had no opportunity to generate a different final configuration than the baseline, explaining the degenerate contingency (n11 = 240, all discordants = 0) and the observed point estimate (0.00) with zero width CI.

Design tradeoffs and consequences for causal measurement: Shared_initial_candidate semantics enforces a directly paired LLM sample and reduces model‑call budget, but it also removes generator variability across arms and thereby makes empirical verifier benefit contingent on the generator producing invalid candidates. If the initial generator seldom violates verifier checks under the chosen model, prompt, and task corpus, the paired contrast will be uninformative. To measure verifier effectiveness as a causal intervention, future confirmatory designs should consider at least one of: (a) independent initial generations per arm (permitting generator variance to create discordance opportunities), (b) stronger or adaptive adversary protocols to increase the chance of invalid shared candidates, or (c) larger repair budgets and iterative repair strategies to exercise the repair search when validation fails. These recommendations are directly motivated by provider_call_audit and validator traces showing identical shared_initial responses and zero repair usage.

Statistical and inference notes: The preregistered power calculation targeted detection of an absolute paired reduction of roughly 8 percentage points with N=240 under assumed baseline rates; realized baseline unsafe rate = 0% leads to a vacuous power analysis for the planned contrast because there were no discordant pairs to test. The bootstrap CI and exact McNemar test are valid for the observed data but illustrate that when realized margin is degenerate the design yields no information about verifier benefit under the executed semantics.

Threats to validity and operational implications: Internal validity: the adapter contract (shared_initial_candidate) is an explicit design choice that constrains causal interpretation—this is not a runtime deviation but a preregistered execution semantics. Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 encodes a finite check set; passing the validator does not guarantee absence of all possible semantic faults. External validity: tasks were drawn from a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus; extrapolation to production, multi‑vendor deployments requires caution. Conclusion validity: the observed baseline success rate of 100% prevents detection of verifier benefit in this design. Operationally, practitioners should not interpret these results as evidence that verifiers are unnecessary; rather, they show that under the chosen model, prompt, task corpus, and shared‑generation semantics every generated candidate satisfied the verifier's checks and so the guarded pipeline was not exercised.

Recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations (artifact‑grounded): (1) To estimate verifier causal effect, avoid shared_initial_candidate semantics or run a mixed design with independent generations per arm so generator variability can create discordances. (2) Increase adversary strength or use adaptive adversaries to create more invalid candidates; the archived adversarial tagging and contamination logic provide a reproducible starting point. (3) Expand repair budgets (allow multiple repair iterations) and instrument repair traces to study search behavior and repair diversity. (4) Broaden verifier coverage and add automated cross‑checks between validator PASS and emulator outcomes to detect potential false‑safe cases; the preregistered contamination plan already envisaged these checks and their automation can be extended.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a GVR pipeline for LLM‑based network configuration. Observed outcome: every paired episode was safe under both arms, yielding a paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the guarded arm could only change the paired outcome by repairing a shared shared_initial candidate that failed deterministic validation; in this run no shared candidate failed validation and no repairs were invoked, producing a degenerate paired contrast. The artifact archive (preregistration, per‑call traces, validator traces, paired contingency, and analysis logs) substantiates these conclusions and supports concrete recommendations for future experiments that seek informative paired contrasts by varying generation semantics, adversary strength, or repair budgets. Our principal methodological lesson is that preregistered execution semantics that minimize generator calls can unintentionally eliminate the empirical opportunity for a validator to demonstrate causal benefit—designers of confirmatory GVR tests must align generator semantics, adversary protocols, and repair budgets to the intended estimand and expected failure modes.

disclosure_statement: Models and tools: Execution used declared model gpt-5-mini via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter; the guarded pipeline used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. Preregistration and autonomy: the study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) and executed under the frozen plan after the autonomy lock. Human role and autonomy boundary: prior to the autonomy lock the human Research Director selected the topic family and constrained the initial master prompt; literature discovery, experiment design, preregistration, execution, analysis, and manuscript drafting occurred autonomously after the lock per track rules. Generation semantics and execution accounting: the registered adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared initial generation per task reused across both arms); therefore only validator‑triggered repairs or validator failures of the shared candidate could create paired divergences. Execution completed per plan: planned_episode_count = 480, completed_episode_count = 480, complete_pair_count = 240, hosted_model_call_event_count = 240, model_calls_used = 240. limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) was tested; results do not imply generality across models, prompts, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed adversary protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.

Verifier coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements a finite set of checks; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected by the verifier, and verifier PASS vs simulator outcome mismatches were planned to be flagged and analyzed (none occurred in this run).
